title: Why Liberals Keep Getting Education Wrong
author: Alexander Nazaryan
summary: Alexander Nazaryan, a former New York teacher, uses the second season of Sold a Story to ask why liberal educators keep getting the fundamentals of teaching wrong. He recounts how Siegfried Engelmann's Direct Instruction was the clear winner of the federal Project Follow Through study yet was never adopted nationwide, partly because its supporters' politics seemed off to progressive critics. He argues that reflexive polarization has long blocked evidence-based reform, noting that 41 percent of K-3 teachers in high-poverty schools remain wary of phonics despite legal mandates in about 40 states. He gives space to skeptics who fear the podcast will be weaponized or that publisher-made curricula will disappoint, and observes that progressives have offered little beyond returning to the old ways. Hanford, in his reading, offers liberals a middle road, and Engelmann's dictum that if the student hasn't learned, the teacher hasn't taught should be uncomfortable for everyone. He closes with his own sense of an aversion to excellence and a fear of failure in public schools. This piece was expanded from Mike Petrilli's roundup of Sold a Story reactions.
points: Direct Instruction beat every other model in Project Follow Through, yet Nazaryan says it was sidelined because its backers' politics seemed wrong rather than because its ideas were bad.
Reflexive polarization is the obstacle to reform: teachers' resistance to phonics was partly resistance to Bush, and 41 percent of K-3 teachers in high-poverty schools still distrust it.
Serious reform energy in education comes from the right, and progressives have offered few alternatives beyond returning to how things used to be.
Curriculum change is hard because corporations produce the materials, teachers need retraining they may resist, and critics fear what Hanford's success will do to the reform conversation.
Nazaryan's own teaching years left him with a sense of an unstated aversion to excellence and a fear of failure that worked like quicksand.
quotes: Sold a Story is for liberals who know that something is wrong with American public education but don’t know what to do about it.
The question that hangs over this podcast like a storm cloud is why educators, and particularly liberal educators, keep getting the fundamentals of teaching wrong.
Engelmann’s supporters’ politics were off, which meant his ideas were bad. And since Kohn gave this assessment in 2022, it seems that little has changed.
Education is one of the few segments of society where the energy for serious reform comes from the right.

Changing a curriculum in a single school — to say nothing of a district or an entire state — is like a restaurant deciding it will transition from smashburgers to omakase. Most teachers need new materials, which are outsourced to corporations that are not necessarily equipped to make them.
Hanford is trying to give liberals a new way to think about public education, a middle road between culture-war minefields. She feels that an enormous amount of time is wasted in schools.

But the podcast also evoked what I found so frustrating about public education, especially in a progressive city like New York. Above all, there was an unstated aversion to excellence, as if urging children to rise to the occasion were asking too much of them.
Even if you’re resistant to Hanford and her message, I ask that you please listen to the first three minutes of Sold a Story’s second season. Literally just three minutes.
